item.title: Kubernetes Architecture: Control Plane, Nodes and Reconciliation
item.description:
Simple definition#

Kubernetes is an open-source platform that runs containerised applications across a cluster of machines. You tell it what you want — “run three copies of this image, reachable on port 8080” — and it continuously works to make the cluster match, restarting, rescheduling and replacing containers as machines and workloads change.

item.title: Running Kubernetes in Practice
item.description:
Simple definition#

“Running Kubernetes” covers day 1 (creating clusters and deploying apps) and day 2 (upgrading, scaling, securing, backing up and operating them for years). Most of the cost and risk of Kubernetes is in day 2.

item.title: Workloads, Scheduling, Autoscaling and Storage
item.description:
Simple definition#

A workload is an application running on Kubernetes. The smallest unit is a Pod — one or more containers that share a network identity and storage. You rarely create Pods directly; you use controllers (Deployment, StatefulSet, DaemonSet, Job) that create and manage Pods for you.

item.title: Kubernetes Networking: Pods, Services, Gateway API and Network Policy
item.description:
Simple definition#

Kubernetes networking answers four questions: how Pods talk to each other, how clients find a stable address for a changing set of Pods (Services), how external traffic gets in (Gateway API / Ingress), and how traffic is restricted (NetworkPolicy).

item.title: Red Hat OpenShift
item.description:
Simple definition#

Red Hat OpenShift is an enterprise Kubernetes platform: certified Kubernetes plus an integrated, supported set of components — operating system, networking, ingress, registry, monitoring, logging, security, CI/CD, GitOps, service mesh, virtualization and a developer portal — installed and upgraded as one product.

item.title: Helm Charts
item.description:
Simple definition#

Helm is the package manager for Kubernetes. A chart is a versioned package of templated Kubernetes manifests; values customise it per environment; installing a chart creates a release that Helm can upgrade and roll back.

item.title: Service Mesh: Istio, Linkerd, Cilium and Ambient Mode
item.description:
Simple definition#

A service mesh is an infrastructure layer that handles service-to-service communication for you: encrypts it with mutual TLS, applies traffic rules (retries, timeouts, canary weights), enforces identity-based authorisation, and emits telemetry — without changing application code.

item.title: System Design: A Highly Available Multi-Region Kubernetes Platform
item.description:
The design brief#

“A digital bank’s customer-facing services (login, accounts, payments) must stay available 24x7 even if an entire cloud region fails. Design the Kubernetes platform and the failover approach.”

1. Requirements and SLOs#

Service tier SLO (availability) RTO RPO
Tier 0: login, balances, payments initiation 99.95% monthly ≤ 15 min regional failover ≤ 1 min (payments ledger: 0 for committed transactions)
Tier 1: statements, notifications 99.9% ≤ 1 h ≤ 15 min
Tier 2: analytics, back-office 99.5% ≤ 24 h ≤ 24 h

Other requirements: EU data residency (two EU regions), PCI DSS scope isolation, peak 3,000 requests/s, deployments several times a day without downtime.

item.title: Kubernetes Security: From Supply Chain to Runtime
item.description:
Simple definition#

Kubernetes security is defence in depth across four layers — the 4Cs: Cloud (accounts, networks), Cluster (API access, policies), Container (images, runtime settings) and Code (dependencies, secrets). A weakness in an outer layer undermines everything inside it.
